title: The city with open gates (Revelation 21:9–27)
hook: the gates are never shut, and the nations bring their glory in

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one on the throne said, behold, I make all things new. Your line was all things new. What did you make new with your own hands? Day one thousand three hundred thirteen.

What's a city wall for? Keeping danger out, and the people inside safe after dark. When Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem's walls, he gave an order: the gates weren't to open until the sun was hot, and the doors were to be shut and barred. In today's passage an angel carries John away to a great high mountain and shows him the holy Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven. It has a wall, great and high. It has twelve gates, and each gate is a single pearl. If you've ever heard of the pearly gates, here they are. And then one line turns the whole idea of a city wall inside out.

First, the names. On the twelve gates, the text says, are written the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel. On the wall's twelve foundations are the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. The city carries both. Second, what's missing. "And I saw no temple therein: for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it." No need of sun or moon either: the glory of God lights it, and the Lamb is its light. A city with no special holy building, because the whole place is near to God. Third, the gates themselves: "And the gates of it shall not be shut at all by day: for there shall be no night there." Put those two halves together. Gates that are never shut by day, in a city where day never ends, are never shut. And look who walks in. "And they shall bring the glory and honour of the nations into it." The kings of the earth come carrying their glory. Two chapters earlier, the kings of the earth were gathered to make war against the rider on the white horse. Now they arrive at an open gate. The prophet Isaiah had pictured something like it: Jerusalem's gates open continually, not shut day nor night, with the wealth of the nations brought in. Fourth, the edge. Verse twenty-seven says nothing that defiles will enter, only those written in the Lamb's book of life. Christians read the open gates and that verse in different ways. Some hear a welcome that reaches very wide. Others hear an open city with a clear standard. The chapter sets them next to each other and lets both stand.
screen: `NO TEMPLE, NO NEED OF THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave a door open. If you can, open one now: a door to the next room, a window, even a cupboard. Then sit where you can see it. Settle, and breathe. Notice the air that moves through, the sounds from the other side. Then bring to mind one person you've quietly closed a gate on. Not someone who's a danger to you; just someone you stopped letting in. You don't have to decide anything. For the length of the sit, picture the gate standing open. If you pray, you can bring their name. If you don't, just breathe by the open door. The bell holds the time.
The city with open gates. Revelation's holy Jerusalem: twelve gates of pearl, no temple, no night, and gates that are never shut.
screen: `THE CITY WITH OPEN GATES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the gates are never shut. Today, leave one real door open for someone: a reply, an invitation, a seat saved at the table. Day one thousand three hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: The phrase 'pearly gates' comes from the gates of pearl in Revelation 21:21, and some churches read the vision of the holy city at funerals and on feasts of dedication.

fork.setup: you're a gate of the holy city. in Nehemiah's Jerusalem, gates stayed shut until the sun was hot. what does Revelation say about you?
options: you're shut and barred, and opened only when the sun is hot.
you're not shut at all by day, and there is no night.
fork.reveal: "the gates of it shall not be shut at all by day: for there shall be no night there." never shut.

original.note: Greek: a gateway, a gate. the word for the twelve gates of the holy city.

trapdoor: what you thought: the pearly gates are where people get checked and turned away.
what it means: twelve gates of pearl that are never shut, and the nations walking in with their glory.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah 60:11 already pictured Jerusalem's gates open continually, not shut day nor night; Revelation 21 picks up that picture.
recall: the first and last Greek letters

notes: Nehemiah 7:3 paraphrased (gates not opened until the sun is hot; shut and barred). Confirm.
Counts (twelve gates, tribes, foundations, apostles) are from Revelation 21:12–14, 21; city measurements deliberately left out.
'Two chapters earlier' refers to Revelation 19:19 (kings of the earth gathered against the rider). Confirm the link is fair.
Two readings of 21:25–27 (wide welcome; open city with a clear standard) given unranked. Confirm.
howItsDone traces the phrase 'pearly gates' to Revelation 21:21 and names funerals and dedication feasts as occasions some churches read the passage; confirm.

Editor: Nehemiah 7:3 no longer says the gates were shut 'at night' (the verse says shut and barred while the watch stands by); 'no sun or moon' changed to 'no need of sun or moon' to match Revelation 21:23; fork and screen lines aligned.
Audit 2026-10-02: quotations (Rev 21:22, 25, 26), Nehemiah 7:3 and Isaiah 60:11 paraphrases and the gate/foundation counts checked; no change.
